headline: Chicory and Joe-Pye Weed on the Bank Mean Night Tide Bass at the River Mouth
subhead: The shad run is a memory now, but the stripers that fed on those fish all spring are still here — you just have to fish them after dark.
body_markdown:
There's a stretch of bank below Ferry Point where the chicory comes up blue and the joe-pye weed goes purple-pink by late July, and I've used that bloom as a clock for fifty years now. When it shows, the river's done with spring. The shad are gone — pushed out and north weeks ago, hickories and American shad both, done with their business in the freshwater above Hartford. What's left is a different river, a slower, heavier, warmer one, and it fishes different too.

Water temp at the mouth has been sitting in the mid-70s on the surface, cooler down in the channel where the salt wedge pushes up against the fresh flow off the dam. That thermal seam — warm river water riding on top of the cooler, saltier bottom layer — is exactly where the bass have been holding through this stretch of settled weather. I've fished this pattern enough summers now to know it doesn't change much once it sets up: stripers go nocturnal, they go deep, and the guys who keep catching through late July are the ones willing to fish the hours nobody wants to fish.

We said as much last week — that the pattern would hold steady with this weather sitting on us, dawn and dusk and the tide changes doing the work — and that's exactly how it's played out. Nothing dramatic, no blitzes, just a consistent, quiet program for anyone willing to work the clock instead of the calendar.

Best fish this week have come off the down-current side of the Baldwin Bridge pilings, fished on the last two hours of the outgoing into the start of the incoming, right around last light into full dark. Guys are drifting live eels back there — a live eel on a 3/0 circle hook, no weight or just enough splitshot to get it down into that seam, let it swing with the current into the shadow line off the pilings. That's produced fish from 24 to maybe 30 inches, nothing huge but a solid, respectable bass in a river that's given up its share of 40-pounders in years past. A few guys throwing bigger bunker chunks off the bottom near the Amtrak trestle have done well too, particularly on the last of the ebb when bait gets flushed down and pinned against the structure.

Great Island continues to be the nursery it's always been this time of year — small bass, schoolies mostly, working the flats and channel edges on both sides of the tide, but especially as that water starts moving on the push of the incoming. If you want numbers over size, that's your spot: white perch mixed in too, especially up in the deeper holes off the Lieutenant River mouth, taking small bucktails and bloodworms fished slow on bottom. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but a fun evening for anybody who wants steady action without needing eels or big bait.

Bluefish have shown at the river mouth proper, right out where the current runs hardest past Saybrook Point and Cornfield Point light, chasing whatever peanut bunker and silversides are getting pushed out of the marsh on the ebb. That's been a daytime thing more than the bass, oddly enough — blues don't seem to mind the warm surface water the way stripers do, and they've been slashing through bait schools out past the breakwater on calm mornings. Small metal — quarter to half-ounce Kastmasters, Deadly Dicks — has worked fine when you can find the surface commotion. It's not the sustained blitz they're seeing to our west in the Sound proper and down toward the city, but it's real, and it's been consistent enough that a few DEP Marina regulars have made it their go-to for an hour of fun before the sun gets too high.

Essex has been quieter than I'd like this week — that stretch above the highway bridge running slow and warm, and without much current to stack bait, the bass haven't shown much interest there in daylight. I'd write it off until we get a little more push in the tide or a cool night knocks the surface temp down a degree or two.

Moon's working toward the next quarter, tides are moderate, nothing extreme in either direction, which means the current isn't doing you any special favors — you need to be in the right spot at the right hour, not relying on a big tidal push to concentrate fish for you. That favors patience over volume. Fish the last light and first dark hours, fish the pilings and the current seams, and don't be afraid to stay out past what feels like a reasonable hour.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break unless we get a real weather change — a strong blow that mixes the water column or a stretch of cooler nights that knocks the surface temp down enough to open up some daytime activity again. Barring that, I'd keep planning trips around dusk into dark, working the bridge structure and the river mouth rips, eel or bunker chunk for the bigger fish, small bucktails up around Great Island if you're happy with schoolies and perch. It's not a fast bite. It's a patient one. That's mid-summer on this river, same as it's always been.
